extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics and philosophy (readers of Kant)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of evaluative criteria and standards for aesthetic judgements (judgement of taste) according to Kant's Critique of Judgement. Focuses on what counts as beauty, purity of taste, purposiveness, and related distinctions (free vs dependent beauty, ideal, normal idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful pleases universally, without a concept
rubrics_metrics.description: "The beautiful is that which pleases universally, without a concept."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgement of beauty must be presented as yielding a satisfaction claim that is communicable to everyone even though it is not grounded in a determinate concept of the object. This universality is not empirical evidence but the claim implicit in the aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as form of purposiveness without a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty is the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The determining ground of judgement of taste is the mere form of purposiveness in the representation (a 'subjective purposiveness') rather than any objective or practical purpose. That is, the object appears as if designed, but no concept of an end (no purpose) is presupposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste rests on the form of purposiveness of the representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judgement of taste has nothing at its basis but the form of the purposiveness (of an object or of its mode of representation)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement concerns how the cognitive faculties relate in the representation (formal purposiveness), not a concept of the object's function or goodness. It rules out grounding the judgement in objective teleology or in representations of the object's utility or perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste is independent of charm and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pure judgement of taste is independent of charm and emotion" (and: "Every interest spoils the judgement of taste and takes from its impartiality").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interests, charms (mere sensory attractiveness), and emotional perturbations contaminate impartial aesthetic judgement. A 'pure' judgement's determining ground must be the formal purposiveness alone; charm or emotion may accompany beauty but cannot be its ground. Antipattern: treating pleasant sensations (colours, tones) as sufficient grounds of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pure (formal) and empirical (material) aesthetic judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgements divide into empirical (assert pleasantness; judgements of sense/material) and pure (assert beauty; formal judgements of taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure judgements concern form and universal communicability; empirical judgements concern sensation and personal pleasantness. Keep the evaluative focus on form (delineation, composition) rather than on merely pleasurable sensory qualities unless those sensory qualities are shown to be 'pure' and contribute to formal unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste has a priori grounds (in the form of subjective purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judgement of taste rests on a priori grounds."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although we cannot establish particular causal links a priori between representation and feeling, the consciousness of a formal purposiveness in the harmonious play of faculties provides an a priori ground for the possibility of a universal claim in aesthetic judgement. This is not an empirical rule but a transcendental account of why such judgements aspire to universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is independent of the concept of perfection or utility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judgement of taste is quite independent of the concept of perfection" (and of objective purposiveness such as utility or internal perfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty should not be reduced to usefulness (external purposiveness) or to the concept of an object's perfection (internal purposiveness conceived by a concept). If satisfaction is grounded in utility or a concept of perfection, the judgement is cognitive/practical rather than purely aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free beauty vs dependent (adherent) beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of beauty: free beauty (pulchritudo vaga) presupposes no concept of what the object ought to be; dependent (adherent) beauty (pulchritudo adhaerens) presupposes such a concept (a purpose) and thus is not purely a judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free beauties (e.g., flowers, abstract designs, wordless music) allow pure aesthetic judgement; dependent beauties (human beauty, buildings, instruments judged by purpose) involve concepts of purpose and may mix aesthetic with cognitive/practical evaluations. A judgement treating a dependent beauty as if free is not 'pure' taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal communicability as a criterion of aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement of taste postulates the universal communicability of the feeling (satisfaction) accompanying the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging something beautiful one implicitly claims that others ought to share the satisfaction. This is an aesthetic claim to valid intersubjective assent, not an empirical generalisation. Empirical agreement across peoples is only weak evidence and not the a priori ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as the felt harmonious play of Imagination and Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure in the judgement of taste is the sensation arising from the excitation of both faculties (Imagination and Understanding) to a harmonious, lively play—this subjective harmony is what is felt and communicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is felt when imagination and understanding engage in a free, mutually agreeable activity; if the representation unites them via a concept (cognitive schematism) it becomes a cognitive judgement, not a pure aesthetic one. Thus evaluate whether pleasure comes from formal cognitive harmony rather than conceptual recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must itself be beautiful in form; finery injures beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament (parerga) augments satisfaction only insofar as it consists in beautiful form; if ornament merely recommends the object by charm (finery), it injures genuine beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing works (frames, draperies, colonnades) distinguish ornament that contributes formal purposiveness from mere decorative finery that distracts by sensory charm. Antipattern: allowing ornaments that have no beautiful form to be taken as evidence of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative arts: delineation/composition (form) is fundamental; colour/tone are charms
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting, sculpture, architecture, horticulture, etc., delineation (form) and composition are essential for pure judgement of taste; colours and tones belong to charm and cannot by themselves establish beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artworks first by their formal delineation and compositional purposiveness. Colours/tones may enliven and aid the intuitability of form but cannot substitute for formal beauty. For nascent taste, charms may be pedagogically useful but should be treated as secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion does not belong to beauty (sublimity uses emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Emotion ... does not belong at all to beauty. But sublimity ... requires a different standard of judgement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional responses (sensations involving a sudden check and stronger outflow of vital force) are distinct from the contemplative pleasure of beauty. When assessing an object, if emotion is the primary ground of satisfaction, the standard in play may be the sublime, not the beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste conditioned by a concept is not pure
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste by which an object is declared beautiful under the condition of a definite concept (i.e., with reference to a purpose) is not a pure judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an aesthetic judgement depends on or presupposes a concept of the object's purpose (e.g., a dwelling-house, a tool), it becomes mixed with cognitive/practical considerations and loses purity. Such judgements may be rule-governed and useful for design, but are not pure aesthetic assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of beauty (human) requires moral expression and combination of normal and rational Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: An Ideal of beauty is possible chiefly for the human figure: it combines a 'normal Idea' (average aesthetic proportions) with a 'rational Idea' that makes moral purposes visible; visible expression of moral Ideas contributes to universally positive pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging human beauty at the level of an Ideal, assess both formal correctness (normal Idea) and whether bodily expression communicates moral qualities (goodness, purity, strength). Such an Ideal is not purely aesthetic in the narrow sense because it invokes moral rational Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Idea as averaged standard of correctness for species
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'normal Idea' is an individual intuition formed by the Imagination averaging many instances (an 'average' figure) that serves as a standard for judging correctness in a species (e.g., human figure, breed-standard of animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of 'correctness' or typical beauty may rely on culturally variable normal Ideas produced by accumulated experience. This explains variation of taste across peoples and the role of an internalised average as a standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any interest (subjective or objective) spoils impartiality of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every interest spoils the judgement of taste and takes from its impartiality..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartial aesthetic judgement must avoid being influenced by personal desires, practical interests, or stakes in the object. If a judging subject has an interest (e.g., economic, moral advantage), the aesthetic claim to universal validity is undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful is thought as having a necessary reference to satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The beautiful we think as having a necessary reference to satisfaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging something beautiful one treats the satisfaction as necessary (i.e., as if it must be so). This modality distinguishes the aesthetic judgement from mere accidental pleasantness; evaluate whether the felt satisfaction is treated as necessary rather than contingent.
